title: JFK (A): Who fired the shots?
question: Who fired the shots that struck President Kennedy and Governor Connally in Dealey Plaza on November 22, 1963?

hypotheses.text: Oswald alone fired all the shots, from the Book Depository's sixth floor
hypotheses.notes: Course Thesis 1 (lone gunman), as concluded by the Warren Commission.

hypotheses.text: Oswald fired, and at least one other gunman also fired (for example from the grassy knoll)
hypotheses.notes: The HSCA's 1979 conclusion (four shots, one from the knoll, which missed) and many conspiracy theses.

hypotheses.text: Oswald fired no shots; he was set up as the fall guy
hypotheses.notes: Oswald's own claim ("I'm just a patsy"); the planted-rifle, planted-bullet and impersonator theories (Syllabus, Appendix V).

evidence.text: A Mannlicher-Carcano rifle (C2766) was found hidden among boxes on the sixth floor; it had been mail-ordered under the alias "A. Hidell" to Oswald's post office box, and handwriting experts matched the order form to Oswald.
evidence.notes: Critics argue the rifle was planted (Syllabus App. V, "Planted-Rifle Theory"); early reports called it a Mauser.

evidence.text: Three spent cartridge cases found by the sixth-floor southeast window were matched to that rifle to the exclusion of all other weapons.
A nearly whole bullet (CE 399, found on a Parkland stretcher) and the two largest fragments from the limousine were matched to the rifle.
evidence.notes: Chain of custody of CE 399 is disputed by critics (Syllabus App. V, "Planted-Bullet Theory").

evidence.text: Oswald's palm print was reported on the rifle's barrel, and prints on the trigger housing were later attributed to him.
evidence.notes: The palm print was lifted by Dallas police and not seen by the FBI at first; critics question when it was taken.

evidence.text: Boxes were stacked into a sniper's perch at the southeast window, screened from the rest of the floor; Oswald's prints were on boxes there.
evidence.notes: Oswald worked on that floor, which can explain prints on boxes.

evidence.text: Witness Howard Brennan saw a man fire a rifle from the sixth-floor southeast window; his later identification of Oswald was hesitant.

Oswald left the Book Depository within minutes of the shooting; about 45 minutes later Officer J.D. Tippit was shot, witnesses identified Oswald, shells at the scene matched the revolver Oswald carried when arrested in the Texas Theatre.
evidence.notes: Bears on consciousness of guilt rather than directly on who fired in Dealey Plaza.

evidence.text: Oswald denied shooting anyone and called himself "just a patsy"; there are no recordings or transcripts of his roughly 12 hours of questioning.
evidence.notes: Credibility here is that he said it, not that it is true.

evidence.text: The autopsy found the President was struck by two bullets from above and behind; review panels in 1968 (Clark), 1975 (Rockefeller) and 1978 (HSCA forensic pathology panel, 8 of 9, Wecht dissenting) agreed.
Parkland Hospital doctors and nurses described the throat wound as an entrance and a large wound at the back of the head, observations that suggest a shot from the front.
evidence.notes: They were treating the President, not examining the wounds forensically; their accounts conflict with each other.

evidence.text: A 1993 JAMA study found trauma specialists misjudged gunshot wounds (entrance vs. exit, number of bullets) in 52% of fatal cases compared with forensic pathologists.
evidence.notes: General reliability evidence; bears on how much weight a10 deserves.

evidence.text: The HSCA's photographic panel tested the autopsy photographs and X-rays and the "backyard" photographs for fakery and found none.
evidence.notes: Directly contrary to body- and photo-alteration claims (Thesis 7).

evidence.text: FBI agents Sibert and O'Neill, present at the Bethesda autopsy, wrote that there had been "surgery of the head area" before the autopsy began.
evidence.notes: The foundation of David Lifton's body-alteration thesis (Thesis 7). Others read it as recording a pathologist's first impression.

evidence.text: Lifton's thesis: the President's wounds were altered before the autopsy to hide shots from the front.
evidence.notes: An inference from a13 and the Parkland accounts, not independent evidence.

evidence.text: Of witnesses who gave an opinion, 81% heard three shots, 12% two, 5% four or more.
Witnesses disagreed about where the shots came from, but very few said they came from more than one direction; Dealey Plaza's buildings produce strong echoes.
Some witnesses reported shots or smoke near the grassy knoll, and people and police ran toward the stockade fence after the shooting.
evidence.notes: No one reported actually seeing a gunman there (Reitzes p. 10).

evidence.text: A search of the grassy knoll and stockade fence area found no weapon, shells or suspect.
The Zapruder film shows the President's head moving back and to the left after the fatal shot.
Rockefeller Commission medical experts (1975) and the HSCA panel attributed the backward motion to a neuromuscular reaction, and noted a brief forward head movement between frames 312 and 313.
evidence.notes: Directly addresses how much weight a19 should carry.

evidence.text: HSCA acoustics consultants concluded from a police Dictabelt recording that four shots were fired, one from the grassy knoll ("95 percent" probability).
evidence.notes: The HSCA's "probable conspiracy" finding rested on this; three committee members dissented (Syllabus p. 14).

evidence.text: The National Academy of Sciences' Ramsey Panel found the Dictabelt sounds were recorded about a minute after the shooting and were not gunshots; the FBI and Justice Department also disputed the HSCA analysis. A later reanalysis (Donald Thomas) disputes the NAS.
The HSCA's photogrammetry (20-expert panel) and trajectory analysis (NASA engineer Thomas Canning) supported the single-bullet explanation; later 3D reconstructions agreed.
evidence.notes: The single-bullet explanation is what makes one gunman's timing possible.

evidence.text: Governor and Mrs. Connally testified in 1964 and again in 1978 that he was hit by a separate bullet from the one that first hit the President.
evidence.notes: Honest eyewitness belief; whether a wounded man can time his own wound is the question.

evidence.text: The Zapruder film limits all the shots to a few seconds; the Warren Commission and HSCA judged three shots from the bolt-action rifle feasible in that time, which critics dispute.
Oswald qualified as a "sharpshooter" (1956) and later "marksman" (1959) in the Marine Corps.
Marina Oswald testified that she took the "backyard" photographs of Oswald holding the rifle and revolver.
evidence.notes: Question 6 asks whether these were faked; see a12.

evidence.text: Marina Oswald testified, supported by documents, that Oswald fired at Gen. Edwin Walker in April 1963.
evidence.notes: Shows willingness and ability to attempt a rifle shooting.

evidence.text: Dallas police paraffin tests were positive on Oswald's hands and negative on his cheek; the test is unreliable and the Warren Commission did not rely on it.
James Tague was slightly wounded by a fragment or ricochet near the triple underpass, showing that at least one shot missed or broke up.
The "three tramps" taken from a boxcar near the knoll were identified from Dallas police files released in 1989 as transients Doyle, Abrams and Gedney.
evidence.notes: Rules out the identifications as Hunt, Sturgis or Harrelson (Question 8).

evidence.text: Figures "found" in enlargements of the Moorman photo ("Badge Man" and others) were judged photographic artifacts; Lifton himself concluded enlargements had very limited value.
The "Umbrella Man" was identified as Louie Steven Witt, who testified to the HSCA that the umbrella was a political protest.
Critics document chain-of-custody gaps and handling problems in key exhibits (the stretcher bullet, the palm print, the autopsy materials).
evidence.notes: Bears on whether a01–a04 could have been planted.
